module_introduction.text:
Hello! This module is about Articles. Articles are the small words 'a', 'an', 'the', or sometimes no article at all (which we call the "zero article"). These words seem small, but they change the meaning of a noun.

Why is this difficult? Because French uses articles all the time, but English sometimes leaves them out. The biggest error is using 'the' for general concepts. In French, you say "Le riz est bon" (Rice is good, in general). In English, you must remove the article: "Rice is good." You cannot say "The rice is good" unless you mean specific rice (e.g., "The rice on my plate"). Also, French "un/une" (a/an) and "des" (some) have different rules. We will practice when to use an article and when not to.

contrastive_explanation.text:
The main problem is that French and English use articles to show "general" vs. "specific" in opposite ways.

A / AN (Indefinite Articles):

The Rule: Use 'a' or 'an' for a single, countable, non-specific noun. It means 'one of many'.

Examples: "I need a pen." (Any pen, not a specific one). "He is a teacher." (His job).

'A' vs. 'An': The rule is about sound, not spelling.

• Use 'a' before a consonant sound: a book, a university (starts with 'y' sound), a European, a uniform.
• Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an apple, an hour (h is silent), an honest man, an MBA (starts with 'em' sound).

French Connection: This is similar to "un / une" ("un stylo", "un professeur"). The main error is forgetting it, especially with jobs (❌ "He is teacher" ➡️ ✅ "He is a teacher").

THE (Definite Article):

The Rule: Use 'the' when the noun is specific. The listener/reader knows which one you are talking about.

Examples: "The teacher (our teacher) is here." "The rice in this bowl is hot."

French Connection: This is similar to "le / la / les". The error is not here, but in the next section.

ZERO ARTICLE (Ø) (No Article):

The Rule: This is the most difficult rule. We use no article when speaking about:

• General Plural Nouns: "I like Ø dogs." (Dogs in general).
• General Uncountable Nouns: "I drink Ø water." (Water in general). "We need Ø information."
• General Abstract Nouns: "Ø Life is short." "Ø Education is important."

French Connection: This is the opposite of French! French requires a definite article for general concepts:

• "J'aime les chiens." (I like dogs) ➡️ ❌ "I like the dogs." ➡️ ✅ "I like Ø dogs."
• "J'aime l'eau." (I like water) ➡️ ❌ "I like the water." ➡️ ✅ "I like Ø water."
• "La vie est courte." (Life is short) ➡️ ❌ "The life is short." ➡️ ✅ "Ø Life is short."

The Error: Students translate "le / la / les" directly to 'the' when talking about general things. You must remember to use zero article for general plurals and uncountables.

common_errors.french_connection: "J'aime le fufu." French uses "le" for a general preference. English must use the zero article (Ø) for general uncountable nouns.

common_errors.wrong: The education is important in Cameroon.
common_errors.correct: Ø Education is important in Cameroon.
common_errors.french_connection: "L'éducation est importante..." French uses "l'" for the general, abstract concept. English must use the zero article.
"Mon père est professeur." French does not use an article for professions after "être". English must use "a/an" for professions.

common_errors.correct: Ngono wants to be a doctor.
common_errors.french_connection: "Elle veut être médecin." English requires the article "a" before professions.

common_errors.wrong: I saw an beautiful kaba (dress) at the market.
common_errors.correct: I saw a beautiful kaba at the market.
common_errors.french_connection: The choice of 'a'/'an' depends on the next sound. 'Beautiful' starts with a 'b' sound (consonant), so we use 'a'.

common_errors.wrong: It takes one hour to go to Douala.
common_errors.correct: It takes an hour to go to Douala.
common_errors.french_connection: The 'h' in 'hour' is silent, so the word starts with a vowel sound ('our'). We must use 'an'.

common_errors.correct: I need some new information. (Or "a piece of...")
common_errors.french_connection: "J'ai besoin d'une information." French treats 'information' as countable. English 'information' is uncountable and cannot use 'a/an'.
"Les étudiants doivent..." French "Les" is used for the general plural (students in general, as a category). English must use the zero article when speaking generally.

common_errors.wrong: I bought a rice from the market.
common_errors.correct: I bought some rice from the market. (Or "a bag of rice")
common_errors.french_connection: "J'ai acheté du riz..." (partitive). 'Rice' is uncountable, so you cannot use 'a'. You must use 'some' or a counter ("a bag").

common_errors.wrong: My brother goes to the school every day.
common_errors.correct: My brother goes to Ø school every day.
common_errors.french_connection: "Mon frère va à l'école..." When talking about going to an institution (school, church, hospital, university) for its main purpose (to learn, to worship, to receive treatment), English uses the zero article (Ø).

form_a_questions.question_text: In general, ___ plantains are expensive in the dry season.
form_a_questions.feedback: Correct! We are talking about 'plantains' in general, not specific plantains. In French, you say "Les bananes...", but in English, we use the zero article (Ø) for general plural nouns.

form_a_questions.question_text: ___ life in Yaoundé is very fast.
form_a_questions.feedback: That's right. We are talking about 'life' as a general, abstract concept. French says "La vie...", but English must use the zero article (Ø).
Excellent! In English, we must use 'a' or 'an' before a singular job or profession. In French, you say "Elle est infirmière" (no article), but this is a mistake in English.
Perfect! The 'h' in 'honest' is silent, so the word starts with a vowel sound ('o'). Therefore, we must use 'an'.

form_a_questions.question_text: I want to go to ___ university in Buea.
form_a_questions.feedback: Good job. This is tricky! 'University' starts with the letter 'u', but it makes a 'y' sound (like 'you-niversity'), which is a consonant sound. So, we use 'a'. (Other examples: a uniform, a European.)

Correct! 'Advice' is uncountable in English (different from French "des conseils"). We cannot use 'a' or 'an'. We use 'some' (or 'a piece of'). (Remember: information, advice, furniture, luggage are all uncountable.)

form_a_questions.question_text: I ate an orange. ___ orange was very sweet.
form_a_questions.feedback: That's it! The first time, you say "an orange" (general). The second time, we know which orange you mean (the one you just mentioned), so it is specific. We must use 'the'.

form_a_questions.question_text: Find the error: "I need to buy a bread."
form_a_questions.correction: some bread (or a loaf of bread)
form_a_questions.feedback: You found it! 'Bread' (le pain) is uncountable. You cannot use 'a' with it. You must say "some bread" or "a loaf of bread".

form_a_questions.question_text: Muna is sick. He is in ___ hospital.
form_a_questions.feedback: Correct! When we talk about going to an institution (like hospital, school, church, prison) for its main purpose (to be a patient, to learn, to worship), we use the zero article (Ø). (Note: In American English, people say "in the hospital", but in British/Cameroonian English, we use zero article.)

form_a_questions.question_text: ___ President of Cameroon is visiting Garoua.
form_a_questions.feedback: Yes! There is only one 'President of Cameroon'. This makes him specific and unique, so we must use 'the'.

form_b_questions.question_text: In my family, we think ___ children should obey their parents.
form_b_questions.feedback: Correct! We are talking about 'children' in general (as a category), not specific children. In French, you say "Les enfants...", but in English, we use the zero article (Ø) for general plural nouns.

form_b_questions.question_text: ___ honesty is a very important quality.
form_b_questions.feedback: That's right. We are talking about 'honesty' as a general, abstract concept. French says "L'honnêteté...", but English must use the zero article (Ø).
Excellent! In English, we must use 'a' or 'an' before a singular job or profession. 'Engineer' starts with a vowel sound, so we use 'an'.

form_b_questions.question_text: It is ___ honour to meet you.
form_b_questions.feedback: Perfect! The 'h' in 'honour' is silent (in British/Cameroonian English), so the word starts with a vowel sound ('o'). Therefore, we must use 'an'.

form_b_questions.question_text: He is ___ European, but he lives in Cameroon.
form_b_questions.feedback: Good job! This is tricky! 'European' starts with the letter 'E', but it makes a 'y' sound (like 'you-ropean'), which is a consonant sound. So, we use 'a'.

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "Do you have an information for me?"
form_b_questions.feedback: You found it! 'Information' is uncountable in English. We cannot use 'a' or 'an' with it. We use 'any' (in questions) or 'some'.

form_b_questions.question_text: I bought a new phone. ___ phone has a good camera.
form_b_questions.feedback: That's it! The first time, you say "a new phone" (general). The second time, we know which phone you mean (the one you just bought), so it is specific. We must use 'the'.

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "My mother bought a furniture."
form_b_questions.correction: some furniture (or a piece of furniture)
form_b_questions.feedback: You spotted it! 'Furniture' is uncountable in English (different from French "des meubles"). You cannot use 'a' with it. You must say "some furniture" or "a piece of furniture".

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "My sister goes to the university in Bamenda."
form_b_questions.feedback: Good catch! When we talk about going to an institution (university, school, church, hospital) for its main purpose (to study, to learn), we use the zero article (Ø). We say "goes to university" not "goes to the university".

form_b_questions.question_text: What is ___ capital of the North-West region?
form_b_questions.feedback: Yes! There is only one capital of the North-West region. This makes it specific and unique, so we must use 'the'.
